extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: A massive multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmark for evaluating multimodal models on college-level problems across six disciplines, with heterogeneous image types and interleaved text-image inputs.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was curated in three stages: selecting subjects based on availability of useful visual inputs, recruiting over 50 university students specializing in those majors to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and create new questions when necessary, and then performing duplicate removal, format/typo checking, and difficulty filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, and lecture materials.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Potential duplicates were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity, then reviewed by authors and removed; problems were standardized for format and typos; very easy problems were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data cleaning included duplicate detection and removal, format and typo checking, and filtering out approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the selected majors collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and created new questions when necessary. Authors then reviewed duplicates, checked formatting and typos, and categorized problems into four difficulty levels. Expert annotators later analyzed sampled GPT-4V errors using their knowledge and golden explanations when available.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors analyzed 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances and categorized root causes into perceptual, lack of knowledge, reasoning, textual understanding, rejection to answer, annotation, and answer extraction errors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors; 90 college senior students were also involved as human experts for evaluation, with 3 student experts per subject.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: A version change log exists in the supplementary material, and the benchmark has a live-updating leaderboard.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Annotator/student attributes include discipline/subject specialization and college senior status.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is motivated by the societal importance of monitoring progress toward Expert AGI, including risks of job displacement and economic disruption, and aims to support development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark may carry curation biases, focuses on college-level subjects, and is not sufficient by itself for testing Expert AGI because there is no direct mapping to the 90th percentile of skilled adults and college exams are not the only relevant tasks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating multimodal models and large multimodal models on zero-shot and few-shot multimodal understanding and reasoning; includes development, validation, and test splits for hyperparameter selection and evaluation.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition [57], because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and “90th percentile of skilled adults,” nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle... The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57].
